dvhandbook-001:
**Key idea:** A driver has three separate obligations: *accept* the item from the sequence, *complete* it on the bus, and *route* the response back to the right sequence. The architecture you pick (serialized, decoupled, or multi-channel) decides when each one happens.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SEQ as sequence
  participant SQR as sequencer
  participant DRV as driver
  participant BUS as DUT pins
  SEQ->>SQR: start_item(req) (wait for grant)
  SEQ->>SQR: finish_item(req)
  DRV->>SQR: get_next_item(req)
  SQR-->>DRV: req
  DRV->>BUS: drive req until handshake
  BUS-->>DRV: rdata / status
  DRV->>DRV: rsp.set_id_info(req)
  DRV->>SQR: item_done(rsp)
  SQR-->>SEQ: finish_item returns
  SEQ->>SQR: get_response(rsp)
```

### Explanation
Interview answer: "I first decide whether the sequence must wait for bus completion. If yes, I use a serialized driver. If not, I decouple acceptance from execution with an owned queue. If the protocol has independent channels or several outstanding transactions, I run one worker thread per channel and track outstanding work by ID."

| Choice | When `item_done` is called | Bus concurrency | Typical protocol |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serialized completion | after the bus transfer completes | one at a time | APB, simple req/ack |
| Decoupled request/response | right after the item is cloned and queued | still one bus thread, sequence runs ahead | slow buses, firmware-like flows |
| Independent channels | on acceptance; responses via `put_response` | one thread per channel, N outstanding by ID | AXI (AW/W/B, AR/R), credit links |

### Code (the three skeletons)
```systemverilog
// 1) Serialized: the sequence waits for bus completion
forever begin
  seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
  rsp = bus_rsp::type_id::create("rsp");
  rsp.set_id_info(req);              // routing: sequence id + transaction id
  drive_to_completion(req, rsp);
  seq_item_port.item_done(rsp);      // exactly one per get_next_item
end

// 2) Decoupled: accept early, complete later
//    accept thread : get_next_item -> clone -> set_id_info -> mailbox.put -> item_done()
//    execute thread: mailbox.get -> drive -> put_response(rsp)

// 3) Independent channels: one thread per channel, pending[id] tracking
fork
  issue_worker();     // records pending[id] BEFORE driving the request
  response_worker();  // matches responses by ID, put_response(rsp)
join
```

### Rules to quote
- `get_next_item()` needs exactly one `item_done()`; `get()` completes the handshake itself, so never call `item_done()` after `get()`.
- Calling `item_done()` early releases the *sequence*; it does not pipeline the *bus*. Pipelining needs independent protocol threads.
- Always `rsp.set_id_info(req)`, or the sequencer routes the response to the wrong sequence (or drops it).
- Only one thread writes a given pin. A reset handler that also drives pins needs an explicit arbiter.
- AXI4-Lite has no IDs, so it completes in order; ID matching is for full AXI4.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Two `item_done` calls cause a UVM error ("item_done called with no outstanding requests").
- Decoupled drivers must clone before `item_done`, or the sequence can mutate the object in flight.
- The sequence must call `get_response()` for every `put_response`, or the response queue overflows (default depth 8).

### Follow-ups
- *Can `finish_item` returning mean the DUT is correct?* No, it only means the driver finished the handshake; the scoreboard decides correctness.
- *How do you pipeline APB?* You don't; APB has no overlap. AHB and AXI pipeline via address/data phases or channels.
dvhandbook-004:
**Key idea:** When channels progress independently (AXI AW, W, B, AR, R) or several transactions are in flight, use one worker per channel and track outstanding work by ID. Register the pending entry *before* driving the request, so an early response always finds it; retire each transaction and credit exactly once. ```mermaid flowchart LR SQR["sequencer"] -->|get_next_item| ACC["acceptor
reserve credit, clone"] ACC -->|queue| ISS["issue worker
alloc ID, record pending"] ISS -->|AW / W / AR| DUT["DUT"] DUT -->|B / R| RSP["response worker
match by ID"] ISS -.->|"pending[id]"| TBL["outstanding table"] RSP -.->|lookup, retire| TBL RSP -->|"put_response(rsp)"| SQR RST["reset owner"] -.->|abort all, reconcile credits| TBL ``` ### Explanation Interview answer: "For an AXI write I fork the AW and W handshakes because either may finish first, then wait for B. For multiple outstanding transactions I split the driver into acceptor, issue worker, and response worker. The issue worker records the transaction by ID before it drives the request." | Ordering rule | Tracking structure | | --- | --- | | In-order completion (no IDs, AXI4-Lite) | one FIFO for reads, one for writes | | At most one active per ID | associative array `pending[id]` | | Several active with the same ID | a FIFO queue per ID (`bus_req q[int][$]`) | | Bursts | beat counter next to each handle | ### Code ```systemverilog task drive_one_write(bus_req req, bus_rsp rsp); fork drive_aw_until_handshake(req); // AW and W may complete in either order drive_w_until_handshake(req); join collect_b_response(rsp); endtask // AXI 4KB rule on INCR bursts (stimulus) constraint no_4k_cross_c { (burst == INCR) -> (((int'(addr[11:0]) >> size) << size) + ((int'(len) + 1) << size)) <= 4096; } // Checker on the AW channel function automatic bit crosses_4k(logic [31:0] a, logic [7:0] len, logic [2:0] size); int unsigned first = (int'(a[11:0]) >> size) << size; return (first + ((int'(len) + 1) << size)) > 4096; endfunction ap_4k: assert property (@(posedge aclk) disable iff (!aresetn) awvalid && awburst == 2'b01 |-> !crosses_4k(awaddr, awlen, awsize)); ``` Worked 4KB case: `addr=0xFF0, size=2 (4 B), len=3` covers 0xFF0..0xFFF, legal. `len=4` adds a beat at 0x1000 and crosses. WRAP bursts are aligned to their total size (max 16 x 128 B = 2 KB) so they never cross; FIXED bursts do not increment. **Valid/ready rule:** a transfer happens on a clock edge with `valid && ready`; the source must not wait for `ready` before raising `valid`, and once high, `valid` and payload stay stable until the transfer. ```wavedrom { "signal": [ { "name": "aclk", "wave": "p......" }, { "name": "valid", "wave": "01...0." }, { "name": "ready", "wave": "0..1.0." }, { "name": "data", "wave": "x=..=x.", "data": ["D0", "D1"] } ], "head": { "text": "D0 transfers in cycle 3, D1 in cycle 4 (valid && ready); payload stable while stalled" } } ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A response in the same cycle as issue: only safe if `pending[id]` was written before the request was driven. - Unknown, duplicate, or stale IDs and a missing/extra `WLAST`/`RLAST` must be flagged by the response worker. - Reset owner: stop accepting, abort every queued and in-flight entry exactly once, return credits, flush scoreboard expectations. ### Follow-ups - *Why 4KB?* It is the smallest region a slave can own; a crossing burst could reach two slaves while the interconnect decodes only the first address. - *Stream signals?* TVALID, TREADY, TDATA, TKEEP (last-beat bytes), TLAST, TUSER.
dvhandbook-005:
**Key idea:** Before coding a testbench, state the *contract* every component agrees on: what the DUT does, what counts as an accepted transfer, what reset cancels, when signals are driven and sampled, and when the test is done. ```mermaid flowchart LR IF["06 apb_if
clocking blocks + SVA"] --> DRV["08 driver"] IF --> MON["10 monitor"] ITEM["07 apb_item"] --> SEQ["09 sequences"] SEQ --> SQR["sequencer"] --> DRV MON -->|analysis port| SCB["11 scoreboard
byte memory model"] ENV["13 env + test
config, objections, watchdog"] --> DRV ENV --> MON ENV --> SCB ``` ### Explanation Interview answer: "Before coding I fix the contract. The target is APB4 with 32-bit aligned word accesses and byte strobes. It behaves like plain memory, errors change nothing, and reset clears everything the model knows. The driver drives on the falling edge and the monitor samples on the rising edge." | Contract | Decision | | --- | --- | | DUT | One APB4 target, 32-bit addr/data, word aligned, 4 byte strobes, PPROT = 0 | | Behavior | Plain memory: write updates enabled bytes only; read returns stored bytes; PSLVERR changes nothing; reset clears the model | | Accepted transfer | Rising edge with `PSEL && PENABLE && PREADY` | | Driver timing | Drives on `negedge` through `drv_cb` | | Monitor timing | Samples on `posedge` with `#1step` input skew | | Reset | Sampled on a rising edge; driver cancels on the next clock, never clears pins from a second thread | | Completion | Test owns the objection; a watchdog catches a stopped clock or stuck transfer | ### Code (build order) ```systemverilog // 1) Compile the interface first // apb_if.sv // 2) One package with all classes package apb_pkg; import uvm_pkg::*; `include "uvm_macros.svh" `include "apb_item.svh" `include "apb_driver.svh" `include "apb_seqs.svh" `include "apb_monitor.svh" `include "apb_scoreboard.svh" `include "apb_env.svh" `include "apb_test.svh" endpackage // 3) Top: DUT, clock, reset, config_db, run_test module tb_top; import uvm_pkg::*; logic pclk = 0, presetn = 0; always #5 pclk = ~pclk; initial begin presetn = 0; repeat (5) @(posedge pclk); presetn = 1; end apb_if vif(pclk, presetn); // apb_mem_dut dut(.pclk, .presetn, .psel(vif.psel), ...); initial begin uvm_config_db#(virtual apb_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.*", "vif", vif); run_test(); end endmodule ``` ### APB facts to quote - A transfer is one setup cycle followed by one or more access cycles; PREADY low extends access and request signals hold steady. - PSLVERR is valid only when PSEL, PENABLE, and PREADY are all high. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A test can pass the driver's own response checks while the monitor and scoreboard find a mismatch: the driver's view of the bus is not independent evidence. - The smoke test must write every byte before reading it, or the model has no expected value. ### Follow-ups - *Why drive on negedge?* Signals settle half a cycle before the DUT samples, which avoids races without relying on skews. - *Where do protocol assertions live?* In the interface, so every test gets them.
dvhandbook-011:
**Key idea:** Keep observation, prediction, comparison, and retirement as separate steps, and never derive the expected value from the output being checked. For a byte-enable memory, model storage as a sparse associative array of bytes and update only strobed lanes.

| Step | Address 0 lanes [3..0] | Expected word |
| --- | --- | --- |
| write `0x11223344`, strb `1111` | 11 22 33 44 | `0x11223344` |
| write `0xAABBCCDD`, strb `0101` | 11 **BB** 33 **DD** | `0x11BB33DD` |
| read addr 0 | compare each byte with `!==` | DUT must return `0x11BB33DD` |

A model that overwrites the whole word predicts `0xAABBCCDD` and reports a false mismatch.

### Explanation
Interview answer: "I model memory as an associative array of bytes indexed by address, so it costs memory only for addresses the test touches. A successful write updates only the bytes whose strobe is set. A read compares each byte with `!==`, so an X from the DUT fails. Reading a byte the test never wrote is an error, not silently accepted."

### Code
```systemverilog
class apb_mem_scoreboard extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(apb_mem_scoreboard)
  uvm_analysis_imp #(apb_item, apb_mem_scoreboard) imp;
  logic [7:0] mem[bit [31:0]];                 // sparse byte memory
  int unsigned observed = 0, reads_checked = 0, errors = 0;

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
    imp = new("imp", this);
  endfunction

  function void write(apb_item t);
    bit [31:0] a;
    if (t.status == APB_RESET) begin             // reset clears the model
      mem.delete();
      return;
    end
    observed++;
    if (t.status != APB_OK) begin
      errors++;
      `uvm_error("BUSERR", "Unexpected error in memory smoke contract")
      return;
    end
    if (t.addr[1:0] != 0 || t.addr > 32'h3fc) begin
      `uvm_error("ADDR", "Address outside modeled contract")
      return;
    end
    if (t.write) begin
      for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++) begin
        a = t.addr + b;
        if (t.strb[b]) mem[a] = t.wdata[8*b +: 8];   // only enabled lanes
      end
    end else begin
      for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++) begin
        a = t.addr + b;
        if (!mem.exists(a))
          `uvm_error("UNINIT", $sformatf("Unknown expected byte %h", a))
        else if (t.rdata[8*b +: 8] !== mem[a])        // X in rdata fails
          `uvm_error("MISMATCH", $sformatf("addr=%h expected=%h actual=%h",
                                           a, mem[a], t.rdata[8*b +: 8]))
      end
      reads_checked++;
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Wider addresses: change the key type, e.g. `logic [7:0] mem[bit [63:0]]`.
- This checks DUT against observed traffic, not that the driver sent what the sequence intended; that needs a separate intent-vs-observed check.
- RO, W1C, RC registers need access-policy prediction (RAL), not plain memory.
- Several writers: define the global order (e.g. what a monitor at the memory port sees), not callback arrival order.
- Expected bus errors: predict the error *and* its side effects (none).

### Follow-ups
- *Why associative over a fixed array?* A 4 GB space with a few touched addresses costs only those entries; `exists()` distinguishes "never written".
- *Why `!==`?* `!=` with X returns X, which an `if` treats as false and hides the bug.
dvhandbook-016:
**Key idea:** Debug by finding the *earliest point of divergence*, not the last symptom. Reproduce exactly (seed, build, options), shrink the stimulus, decide whether the DUT, the monitor, or the model is wrong, then lock the fix in with a regression test. ```mermaid flowchart TB F["failure: mismatch / hang / X / flaky"] --> R["record seed, test, simulator version,
options, source revision"] R --> REP["reproduce, then shrink stimulus"] REP --> D["compare failing vs passing run
at transaction boundaries"] D --> W{"who is wrong?"} W -->|DUT| FIX1["file RTL bug"] W -->|monitor sampling| FIX2["fix TB sampling"] W -->|reference model| FIX3["fix model"] FIX1 --> T["add targeted regression test"] FIX2 --> T FIX3 --> T ``` ### Sample answer (STAR) | | | | --- | --- | | **Situation** | A nightly regression showed a read-data mismatch on one seed in a memory controller. | | **Task** | Find the root cause and stop it recurring. | | **Action** | Reproduced with the same seed and build, dumped transactions around the first mismatch, found the model ignored byte enables on a partial write; the DUT was correct. Fixed the model, added a partial-strobe directed test and a coverage bin for strobe patterns. | | **Result** | Seed passed, the new bin showed the case had never been covered, and two more partial-write corner cases were found that week. | ### Checklists to quote | Symptom | Look at | | --- | --- | | Hang | raised objections (`+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE`), blocked threads, pending bus transfers, non-empty scoreboard queues; usual causes: missing `item_done`, `wait` on an event that already fired, zero-delay loop | | Cannot reproduce | different build, different seed source, a race between processes, uninitialized state | | X propagation | uninitialized regs/memories, multiple drivers, undriven inputs, out-of-range array reads, power-down domains, `case` without `default` | | CPUs read inconsistent data | coherence: missing invalidation, write-back not completed, missing barrier; trace each core's line state | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The DUT is right but the monitor sampled the wrong cycle. - The model ignores byte enables. - Same seed, different result on a different build: random stability changed because code was added before the randomize call. ### Follow-ups - *How do you shrink a failing test?* Cut transactions before the first divergence, constrain the address range, replay with a directed sequence. - *How do you prove the fix?* The original seed passes and the new targeted test fails on the old code.
dvhandbook-022:
**Key idea:** Every spawned process needs an owner, a completion condition, and a cleanup rule. `join` waits for all, `join_any` for the first, `join_none` for none. For a timeout, race the work against a delay with `join_any`, then `disable fork`, all wrapped in an outer `fork ... join` so only those two threads are killed.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  P["parent"] --> OF["outer fork ... join (isolation)"]
  OF --> IF["inner fork ... join_any"]
  IF --> W["do_work()"]
  IF --> T["#TIMEOUT then uvm_error"]
  W -->|first to finish| DF["disable fork: kills only the losing sibling"]
  T -->|first to finish| DF
  DF --> R["parent continues"]
```

| Construct | Parent continues when |
| --- | --- |
| `fork ... join` | all children finish |
| `fork ... join_any` | first child finishes (others keep running) |
| `fork ... join_none` | immediately |
| `wait fork` | all children of the current process finish |
| `disable fork` | kills all active children of the current process |

### Code
```systemverilog
task automatic run_with_timeout(time TIMEOUT);
  fork
    begin                               // isolation: disable fork stays inside
      fork
        do_work();
        begin
          #TIMEOUT;
          `uvm_error("TIMEOUT", "Operation exceeded latency bound")
        end
      join_any
      disable fork;
    end
  join
endtask

// Loop variable capture
initial begin
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
    automatic int k = i;                // each thread gets its own copy
    fork
      run(k);
    join_none
  end
  wait fork;
end

// Continue after any two of three tasks
task automatic two_of_three();
  int done_cnt = 0;
  fork
    begin task_a(); done_cnt++; end
    begin task_b(); done_cnt++; end
    begin task_c(); done_cnt++; end
  join_none
  wait (done_cnt >= 2);
  after_two();
endtask

// Kill one branch: named block or process handle
initial begin
  process p;
  fork
    begin : b2 long_task(); end
    begin p = process::self(); other_task(); end
  join_none
  #100;
  disable b2;
  wait (p != null);
  p.kill();
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without `automatic int k`, all three threads see the final `i == 3`.
- `disable fork` without the outer wrapper also kills unrelated threads the same parent started earlier.
- A killed thread holding a semaphore key or credit does not return it; release in the parent after `disable fork`.
- The task and the timeout finishing in the same time step: order is undefined; decide which wins.
- `wait fork` also waits for threads you did not mean to include (e.g. earlier `join_none`).

### Follow-ups
- *Print order of nested join_any with delays?* Trace each thread's absolute time; `join_any` returns at the smallest finish time, other threads keep printing later unless disabled.
dvhandbook-023:
**Key idea:** A handle, the object it points to, and that object's real type are three different things. Assigning handles shares one object; `copy`/`clone` makes a new one (nested objects stay shared unless `do_copy` deep-copies them). A `virtual` method dispatches on the real object type; a non-virtual one on the handle's declared type. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["shape s (handle)"] --> OBJ["circle object
r = 1"] C["circle c (handle)"] --> OBJ OBJ --> CFG["nested cfg object"] CL["clone of c"] --> OBJ2["new circle object"] OBJ2 -->|shallow copy shares| CFG ``` ### Code ```systemverilog class shape; virtual function real area(); return 0; endfunction function string kind(); return "shape"; endfunction // NOT virtual endclass class circle extends shape; real r; virtual function real area(); return 3.14159*r*r; endfunction function string kind(); return "circle"; endfunction endclass module tb; shape s; circle c; initial begin c = new; c.r = 1; s = c; // upcast: always legal $display("%f", s.area()); // 3.141590: virtual uses real type $display("%s", s.kind()); // "shape": non-virtual uses handle type if (!$cast(c, s)) $error("not a circle"); // downcast checked at run time end endmodule // Pass by value vs ref function automatic void f_val(circle h); h = new; h.r = 5; endfunction // caller unchanged function automatic void f_ref(ref circle h); h = new; h.r = 5; endfunction // caller now points to new object // Singleton class cfg_singleton; static protected cfg_singleton inst; protected function new(); endfunction static function cfg_singleton get(); if (inst == null) inst = new(); return inst; endfunction endclass // Abstract base virtual class base_drv; pure virtual task drive(int data); endclass ``` | Operation | New object? | Nested objects | | --- | --- | --- | | `b = a` | no, same object | shared | | `b = new a` (shallow copy) | yes | shared | | `b.copy(a)` / `clone()` with deep `do_copy` | yes | copied | ### Rules to quote - Check every `$cast` on a downcast; it returns 0 on failure (task form is fatal). - SV supports override (same signature in a subclass), not overloading by argument type as in C++. - `uvm_component` is static, has a parent and phases; `uvm_object` is transient data (items, sequences, configs). ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Two queue entries point to one mutable object: modifying one changes "both". - A copied object still shares a nested object. - A missing `virtual` keyword in the base silently breaks polymorphism. - Passing a handle by value still lets the callee modify the *object*. ### Follow-ups - *Why is the constructor not virtual?* `new` is resolved by the declared class being constructed; use the factory to get polymorphic creation.
dvhandbook-024:
**Key idea:** State holds only the history the future needs. For a pattern detector, each state is "the longest suffix of the input so far that is also a prefix of the pattern", so a mismatch falls back to that suffix, not to idle. Ask first: Mealy or Moore, overlapping or not.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> S0
  S0 --> S0: 0/0
  S0 --> S1: 1/0
  S1 --> S0: 0/0
  S1 --> S2: 1/0
  S2 --> S2: 1/0
  S2 --> S3: 0/0
  S3 --> S0: 0/0
  S3 --> S1: 1/1
```

Overlapping 1101 Mealy detector (S0 "", S1 "1", S2 "11", S3 "110"). After "1101" the last 1 starts a new match, so S3 with input 1 goes to S1.

### Code
```systemverilog
module det1101 (input logic clk, rst_n, din, output logic dout);
  typedef enum logic [1:0] {S0, S1, S2, S3} state_e;
  state_e state, next;

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)      // state register
    if (!rst_n) state <= S0;
    else        state <= next;

  always_comb begin                               // next-state logic
    next = state;
    unique case (state)
      S0: next = din ? S1 : S0;
      S1: next = din ? S2 : S0;
      S2: next = din ? S2 : S3;
      S3: next = din ? S1 : S0;
    endcase
  end

  assign dout = (state == S3) && din;             // Mealy output

  // Check against a shift-register reference
  logic [3:0] hist;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) hist <= '0; else hist <= {hist[2:0], din};
  int n;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) n <= 0; else if (n < 4) n <= n + 1;
  ap_ref: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    n >= 3 |-> dout == ({hist[2:0], din} == 4'b1101));
endmodule
```

### Serial divisibility by 5 (MSB first)
r_next = (2r + bit) mod 5, one state per remainder:

| r | bit 0 | bit 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 4 | 3 | 4 |

Trace "1010" (10): 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0 -> 0, divisible. LSB first also needs the current power of 2 mod N.

### Rules to quote
| | Moore | Mealy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Output depends on | state only | state and input |
| Timing | one cycle later, glitch-free | same cycle |
| States for 1101 | 5 | 4 |

A shift-register detector compares the last N bits directly and costs N flops.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Falling back to S0 on every mismatch misses "11101" (S2 on 1 must stay S2).
- Non-overlapping variant: S3 on 1 outputs 1 and goes to S0.

### Follow-ups
- *Two patterns at once?* Build a combined state set (Aho-Corasick style) or two detectors in parallel.
dvhandbook-026:
**Key idea:** Choose a CDC mechanism that keeps the *information* correct, not one that merely moves bits. Single stable level: 2-flop synchronizer. Pulse from fast to slow: toggle/stretch or handshake. Multi-bit value: handshake with stable data or an async FIFO. Synchronizing each bit of a bus separately is wrong. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph WD["write clock domain"] WB["wbin"] --> WG["wgray"] WFULL["full = wgray_next vs synced rgray
(top 2 bits inverted)"] end subgraph RD["read clock domain"] RB["rbin"] --> RG["rgray"] REMPTY["empty = rgray_next == synced wgray"] end WG -->|2-flop sync| REMPTY RG -->|2-flop sync| WFULL WB -->|waddr| MEM["dual-port RAM"] RB -->|raddr| MEM ``` | What crosses | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Stable single-bit level | 2- or 3-flop synchronizer | | Pulse, fast to slow | toggle or stretch + synchronizer, or req/ack | | Multi-bit value | handshake with stable data, or async FIFO | | Continuous stream | dual-clock FIFO | ### Code ```systemverilog module async_fifo #(parameter int DW = 8, parameter int AW = 4) ( // AW >= 2 input logic wclk, wrst_n, winc, input logic [DW-1:0] wdata, output logic wfull, input logic rclk, rrst_n, rinc, output logic [DW-1:0] rdata, output logic rempty ); logic [DW-1:0] mem [2**AW]; logic [AW:0] wbin, wgray, rbin, rgray; // N+1 bit pointers logic [AW:0] wq1_rgray, wq2_rgray, rq1_wgray, rq2_wgray; logic [AW:0] wbin_n, wgray_n, rbin_n, rgray_n; // ---------------- write domain ---------------- assign wbin_n = wbin + (winc & ~wfull); assign wgray_n = (wbin_n >> 1) ^ wbin_n; always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n) if (!wrst_n) begin wbin <= '0; wgray <= '0; wfull <= 1'b0; end else begin wbin <= wbin_n; wgray <= wgray_n; wfull <= (wgray_n == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]}); end always_ff @(posedge wclk) if (winc && !wfull) mem[wbin[AW-1:0]] <= wdata; always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n) // sync read pointer if (!wrst_n) {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= '0; else {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= {wq1_rgray, rgray}; // ---------------- read domain ---------------- assign rbin_n = rbin + (rinc & ~rempty); assign rgray_n = (rbin_n >> 1) ^ rbin_n; always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n) if (!rrst_n) begin rbin <= '0; rgray <= '0; rempty <= 1'b1; end else begin rbin <= rbin_n; rgray <= rgray_n; rempty <= (rgray_n == rq2_wgray); end assign rdata = mem[rbin[AW-1:0]]; always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n) // sync write pointer if (!rrst_n) {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= '0; else {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= {rq1_wgray, wgray}; endmodule ``` ### Rules to quote - Gray code changes one bit per increment, so a pointer sampled mid-change is the old or the new value, never a wrong one. - Full/empty are *pessimistic*: the synchronized pointer is stale, so full may stay asserted a few cycles too long and empty may deassert late; neither causes overflow or underflow. - MTBF = e^(t_r/tau) / (T0 x f_clk x f_data). Each extra flop adds a full cycle to t_r, raising MTBF exponentially. - SDC: `set_max_delay -datapath_only ` on Gray pointer bits so they arrive within one destination period; `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` for the rest. - Same frequency with unknown phase still needs CDC. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A pulse too short for the receiving clock is lost; events faster than the toggle handshake can carry collapse. - Independently synchronized binary bits can form a word that never existed (0111 -> 1000 seen as 1111). - Reset reaching only one side leaves stale pointers; reset both domains together. ### Follow-ups - *Why N+1-bit pointers?* The extra MSB distinguishes full (wrapped once) from empty (equal).
dvhandbook-027:
**Key idea:** Draw the launch and capture edges before any equation. Setup checks that data launched on one edge arrives before the *next* capture edge; hold checks that new data does not arrive too soon after the *same* edge. Lowering frequency fixes setup but never hold, because the hold check does not depend on the period.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk_launch",  "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "clk_capture", "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "Q1 (launch)", "wave": "x=.=.", "data": ["D0", "D1"] },
  { "name": "D2 (arrive)", "wave": "x.=.=", "data": ["D0", "D1"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "setup: arrival before next capture edge; hold: new data not before hold window of same edge closes" } }
```

With skew = capture latency minus launch latency:

| Check | Inequality | Depends on T_clk? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup | T_clk + T_skew >= T_cq,max + T_comb,max + T_setup + T_unc | yes |
| Hold | T_cq,min + T_comb,min >= T_hold + T_skew + T_unc | no |

Worked example: T_cq = 0.2, T_comb,max = 3.5, T_setup = 0.1, skew = 0, uncertainty 0.2 ns gives T_clk >= 4.0 ns, f_max = 250 MHz. With T_comb,min = 0.05, T_hold = 0.1, skew = 0.3: 0.25 >= 0.6 fails hold by 0.35 ns; slowing the clock does nothing, add 0.35+ ns of delay cells.

### Fixes
- **Setup:** shorten logic, pipeline, faster cells, useful skew, lower frequency.
- **Hold:** add delay on the data path. Positive skew helps setup and hurts hold.

### Code
```systemverilog
// Divide-by-3 with 50% duty cycle
module div3 (input logic clk, rst_n, output logic clk_div3);
  logic [1:0] cnt;
  logic p, n;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) cnt <= '0; else cnt <= (cnt == 2) ? 2'd0 : cnt + 2'd1;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) p <= 1'b0; else p <= (cnt == 0);   // high 1 of 3 cycles
  always_ff @(negedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) n <= 1'b0; else n <= p;            // same pulse, half cycle later
  assign clk_div3 = p | n;                         // high for 1.5 of 3 cycles
endmodule
```
```tcl
create_generated_clock -name clk_div3 -source [get_ports clk] -divide_by 3 [get_pins u_or/Y]
```

### Rules to quote
- **Clock gating:** a plain AND glitches if enable changes while clk is high. An ICG latches enable while clk is low (negative-level latch), then ANDs, so enable only changes when the output is already low.
- **Clock mux:** `sel ? clk1 : clk2` can produce a runt pulse. A glitch-free mux uses one enable flop per clock, each on its own falling edge, with cross-coupled feedback, so one enable turns off before the other turns on.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clock dividers built from logic need `create_generated_clock`, or STA treats the output as data.
- Multi-cycle paths need both setup and hold multicycle constraints adjusted.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does positive skew help setup?* The capture edge arrives later, giving the data more time; it also delays the hold window by the same amount.
dvhandbook-031:
**Key idea:** Dynamic power is alpha C V^2 f, so voltage helps most; clock gating cuts switching, multi-Vt and power gating cut leakage. Every power-down and power-up step has a defined order, and verification must prove no corrupted (X) value leaks from an off domain into always-on logic.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph DOWN["power down"]
    D1["stop clocks"] --> D2["enable isolation"] --> D3["save retention"] --> D4["switch off"]
  end
  subgraph UP["power up"]
    U1["switch on, wait stable"] --> U2["restore retention"] --> U3["release reset"] --> U4["disable isolation"] --> U5["start clocks"]
  end
  D4 --> U1
```

| Technique | Saves | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clock gating | dynamic | no glitches, enable timing, same function gated or not |
| Operand isolation | dynamic | idle datapath inputs held constant |
| Multi-Vt | leakage | timing only |
| Power gating | leakage | isolation clamps, retention save/restore, reset on power-up, no X leakage |
| Multiple voltages | dynamic | level shifter on every crossing |
| DVFS | both | raise V before f when speeding up; lower f before V when slowing |

### Code
```tcl
create_power_domain PD_CORE -elements {u_core}
create_supply_net VDD_CORE
set_isolation iso_core -domain PD_CORE -applies_to outputs \
    -clamp_value 0 -isolation_signal iso_en -isolation_sense high
set_retention ret_core -domain PD_CORE \
    -save_signal {save high} -restore_signal {restore high}
```
```systemverilog
// Power-sequence checks (in a bind module)
ap_iso_before_off: assert property (@(posedge clk_aon) disable iff (!rst_aon_n)
  $fell(core_pwr_on) |-> iso_en);
ap_iso_until_reset: assert property (@(posedge clk_aon) disable iff (!rst_aon_n)
  !core_pwr_on |-> iso_en);
ap_no_x_leak: assert property (@(posedge clk_aon) disable iff (!rst_aon_n)
  iso_en |-> !$isunknown(core_out_isolated));
```

### Safety, security, memories
- **Safety:** parity/ECC on storage and buses, duplication/TMR with voting, watchdogs, defined safe state. Lockstep runs two cores a few cycles apart and compares every cycle (about 2x core area and power plus a comparator).
- **Security:** lock bits after boot, no production debug backdoors, clear secrets on reset and mode change, FSMs that recover from illegal states, constant-time operations on secrets.
- **SRAM:** single-port does one access per cycle, dual-port two at more area. No reset (too costly per bit), so software or BIST initializes it and the testbench must not read before write. Bank large memories and enable only the accessed bank (shorter bitlines, less energy).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Isolation released before reset/restore lets X escape for a cycle.
- Retention restore before supply is stable restores garbage.
- Power-aware simulation corrupts off-domain state to X; a test that passes without UPF proves nothing about sequencing.

### Follow-ups
- *Why lower f before V when slowing?* Lowering V first makes the current f too fast for the slower logic, causing setup failures.
dvhandbook-032:
**Key idea:** The stored state must support exactly the queries and updates the problem asks for. Ask about input size, memory, duplicates, and ties first; pick the structure from the operations; state time and space complexity before coding.

| Requirement | Method | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lookup, counting, uniqueness | hash map / set | O(n) time, O(n) space |
| Fixed-length rolling sum | add entering, subtract leaving | O(n), O(1) |
| Longest valid substring | sliding window with maintained condition | O(n) |
| Maximum subarray | Kadane: best ending here, best overall | O(n), O(1) |
| K smallest / kth smallest in a stream | max-heap of size K | O(n log K), O(K) |
| Interval merge | sort by start, merge overlaps | O(n log n) |
| Pair from both ends | two pointers on sorted data | O(n log n) |
| Grid diagonals | group cells by i + j (or i - j) | O(rows x cols) |
| Parse/filter logs | split, regex, bounded buffers | O(lines) streaming |

Kadane trace on `[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]`:

| x | -2 | 1 | -3 | 4 | -1 | 2 | 1 | -5 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| best ending here | -2 | 1 | -2 | 4 | 3 | 5 | **6** | 1 | 5 |
| best overall | -2 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **6** | 6 | 6 |

### Code
```python
import heapq, re

def kadane(a):
    best = cur = a[0]                     # works for all-negative input
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def kth_smallest_stream(stream, k):
    heap = []                             # max-heap via negation, size <= k
    for x in stream:
        if len(heap) < k:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -x)
        elif x < -heap[0]:
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, -x)
    return -heap[0] if len(heap) == k else None

def merge_intervals(iv):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(iv):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out

def longest_unique_substring(s):
    last, start, best = {}, 0, 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        if c in last and last[c] >= start:
            start = last[c] + 1
        last[c] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best

# One-liners interviewers expect
# names     = [s.strip() for s in line.split(",") if s.strip()]
# errors    = [l for l in open(path) if re.search(r"\bERROR\b", l)]
# no_vowels = "".join(c for c in s if c.lower() not in "aeiou")
# by_value  = sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Kadane on all-negative arrays must return the largest single value, not 0.
- Ties at K, duplicates, and confusing kth smallest with kth largest.
- Input larger than memory: stream line by line, keep bounded state.
- Elevator cargo with at most two items per trip: sort and pair heaviest with lightest that fits (two pointers). With unlimited items per trip it is bin packing (NP-hard), so ask for constraints.

### Follow-ups
- *Single-elimination bracket with n players?* Always n - 1 matches (each eliminates one player).
- *Longest consecutive sequence in O(n)?* Put all values in a set; start counting only at x where x-1 is absent.
dvhandbook-034:
**Key idea:** State the cache geometry, who owns the latest data, and the ordering model before walking a trace. Split the address into tag, index, and offset; track each core's line state for coherence; classify pipeline hazards by dependency type.

Worked case: 32 KB, 4-way, 32-byte lines, 32-bit address.

| Field | Formula | Bits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| offset | log2(32) | 5 |
| sets | 32768 / (32 x 4) = 256 | |
| index | log2(256) | 8 |
| tag | 32 - 8 - 5 | 19 |

Address `0x1234_5678`: offset = `0x18`, index = `0xB3`, tag = `0x091A2`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> I
  I --> E: read miss, no sharers
  I --> S: read miss, others have copy
  I --> M: write miss (invalidate others)
  E --> M: local write (silent)
  S --> M: local write (invalidate others)
  M --> S: remote read (supply data, write back)
  E --> S: remote read
  M --> I: remote write
  S --> I: remote write
  E --> I: remote write
```

MESI. MOESI adds **O** (dirty and shared): on a remote read, M goes to O and supplies data without writing back to memory.

### Explanation
| State | Dirty | Copies | Can write without bus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | yes | only | yes |
| O | yes | shared, this cache supplies | no |
| E | no | only | yes (becomes M) |
| S | no | maybe shared | no |
| I | - | - | no |

Two processors writing the same line: one wins ownership (others invalidated), then the second write takes ownership in turn.

### Pipeline and OoO
- **RAW** is a true dependency: forwarding or stall. Load-use still stalls one cycle in a classic 5-stage pipeline.
- **WAR/WAW** appear only with out-of-order execution: register renaming.
- **ROB** commits in program order for precise exceptions; the **RAT** maps architectural to physical registers; a checkpoint copy restores the RAT after a mispredict.
- **Replacement:** true LRU over 16 ways needs a full order; tree PLRU needs 15 bits per set, flipped away from the accessed way.
- **Write-back** writes memory on dirty eviction; **write-through** on every store.
- **Interrupts:** finish current instruction, save context, jump to handler, handler clears the source (often W1C), return. Ask level vs edge, masking, priority.
- **Jump immediate** encodes the target; **jump register** reads it from a register (returns, computed jumps).

### Code
```systemverilog
// Address split as SV functions (parameterized geometry)
localparam int LINE = 32, WAYS = 4, SIZE = 32768, AW = 32;
localparam int OFF  = $clog2(LINE);
localparam int IDX  = $clog2(SIZE / (LINE * WAYS));
localparam int TAG  = AW - IDX - OFF;
function automatic logic [IDX-1:0] index_of(logic [AW-1:0] a); return a[OFF +: IDX]; endfunction
function automatic logic [TAG-1:0] tag_of  (logic [AW-1:0] a); return a[AW-1 -: TAG]; endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Non-power-of-two sets make the index a modulo, not a bit slice.
- Inconsistent reads across CPUs: suspect a missing invalidation, an incomplete write-back, or a missing barrier.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does MOESI help?* Dirty sharing avoids a memory write-back on every read of a modified line.
dvhandbook-035:
**Key idea:** Decide each transistor's operating region before applying an equation. In a CMOS gate the NMOS network pulls down and the PMOS network pulls up as duals: NAND has NMOS in series (output low only when all inputs are high) and PMOS in parallel (any low input pulls high). Series devices are widened to match the reference inverter's drive.

| A | B | NMOS (series) | PMOS (parallel) | Y = NAND |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | off | both on | 1 |
| 0 | 1 | off | one on | 1 |
| 1 | 0 | off | one on | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | both on | off | 0 |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  VDD["VDD"] --> PA["PMOS A"]
  VDD --> PB["PMOS B"]
  PA --> Y["Y"]
  PB --> Y
  Y --> NA["NMOS A"]
  NA --> NB["NMOS B"]
  NB --> GND["GND"]
```

### Explanation
1. Find Vgs and Vds for each device.
2. Check threshold voltage and body effect (stacked NMOS sources sit above ground, raising Vt).
3. Analyze pull-up and pull-down paths, switching threshold, noise margins.
4. Add parasitic capacitance, charge sharing, and leakage where they matter.

**NAND2 sizing:** reference inverter NMOS 1, PMOS 2. Two series NMOS each need width 2 (so the stack equals 1); PMOS are in parallel and the worst case is one on, so each stays width 2.

### Worked numbers
| Item | Formula | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RC low-pass | H(s) = 1 / (1 + sRC) | |
| Cutoff | f_c = 1 / (2 pi R C) | R = 1 kOhm, C = 1 uF: f_c = 159 Hz |
| At f_c | gain -3 dB, phase -45 deg | |
| Above f_c | -20 dB per decade | 1.59 kHz: about -20 dB |
| Step response | V (1 - e^(-t/RC)) | 63% at t = RC = 1 ms |
| Electromigration | MTTF = A J^-n exp(Ea / kT) | average current for DC wear-out, RMS for self-heating |

```python
import math
R, C = 1e3, 1e-6
fc = 1 / (2 * math.pi * R * C)          # 159.15 Hz
gain_db = lambda f: -10 * math.log10(1 + (f / fc) ** 2)
print(round(fc, 2), round(gain_db(fc), 2), round(gain_db(10 * fc), 2))  # 159.15 -3.01 -20.04
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A device assumed saturated is really in the linear region (check Vds >= Vgs - Vt).
- Charge sharing on a dynamic node after precharge changes its voltage.
- Leakage breaks an ideal static assumption (e.g. a floating node drifts).
- **Latch-up:** a parasitic PNPN thyristor between wells shorts supply to ground; prevent with well taps, guard rings, spacing.
- NMOS pass gate passes a weak 1 (VDD - Vt); a chain does not lose more than one Vt if gates are at VDD.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is NOR slower than NAND?* NOR has series PMOS, and PMOS mobility is lower, so it needs much wider devices.
dvhandbook-036:
**Key idea:** A behavioral story shows decisions *you* made, with evidence and a number. A puzzle answer removes possibilities under stated rules, and starts by confirming the rules.

### Story order
Context, your responsibility, options you saw, trade-off you chose, result with a number, what you would do differently.

| STAR | Sample answer: "an interesting bug" |
| --- | --- |
| **Situation** | Block-level regression for a DMA engine passed, but one long random test hung at 2% of seeds. |
| **Task** | I owned the DMA testbench and had to decide whether it was a DUT or TB issue before tape-out review. |
| **Action** | Reproduced with the seed, traced the first divergence (no response for descriptor 37), found the DUT dropped a descriptor when a 4KB-crossing transfer coincided with a channel abort. Chose a directed test plus a coverage cross (abort x boundary) over just adding seeds. |
| **Result** | RTL fix in two days; the new cross exposed one more abort bug; seed failure rate went to 0 over 5,000 seeds. Next time I would add abort-timing crosses from the start. |

### Puzzles
**Lighter stone among 9 (2 weighings):**

| Weighing | Compare | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | group A (3) vs group B (3) | lighter side holds it; balanced means group C |
| 2 | stone 1 vs stone 2 of that group | lighter one is it; balanced means stone 3 |

Ask first whether the odd stone is known to be lighter; an unknown direction changes the method (12 stones, 3 weighings is the classic).

**100 switches:** pass k toggles every kth switch, so switch n toggles once per divisor of n. Divisors pair up except for perfect squares, so only squares end ON: 1, 4, 9, ..., 100, which is **10 switches**.

| n | divisors | toggles | final |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | 1, 2, 3, 6 | 4 | OFF |
| 9 | 1, 3, 9 | 3 | ON |
| 12 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 | 6 | OFF |
| 16 | 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 | 5 | ON |

```python
on = [n for n in range(1, 101)
      if sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if n % k == 0) % 2]
print(on, len(on))   # [1, 4, 9, ..., 100] 10
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- "We" stories hide your contribution; say "I" and name your decision.
- No number in the result makes the story unverifiable; give bugs found, coverage, or time saved.
- For "proudest project", pick one where you personally made a design decision.

### Follow-ups
- *What would you do differently?* Always have one concrete answer ready.
- *Why two weighings suffice for 9?* Each weighing has three outcomes, and 3^2 = 9.
chipverify-003:
**Key idea:** `new()` is the plain SystemVerilog constructor: it always builds exactly the declared class. `type_id::create()` asks the UVM factory for an object, so the factory can return a *derived* type if a type or instance override is registered, without editing the code that calls `create()`. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["drv = my_driver::type_id::create(drv, this)"] --> F{"factory: override
for my_driver at this path?"} F -->|no| B["new my_driver"] F -->|"yes: err_driver"| D["new err_driver (derived)"] N["drv = new(drv, this)"] --> B2["always my_driver"] ``` | | `new()` | `type_id::create()` | | --- | --- | --- | | Defined by | SystemVerilog | UVM factory (needs `` `uvm_*_utils ``) | | Overrides honored | no | yes (type and instance) | | Instance path known | no | yes (name + parent gives full path for instance overrides) | | Typical use | ports (`ap = new("ap", this)`), covergroups, plain classes | components, sequence items, sequences, configs | ### Code ```systemverilog class my_env extends uvm_env; `uvm_component_utils(my_env) my_driver drv; function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); super.build_phase(phase); drv = my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this); // overridable // drv = new("drv", this); // NOT overridable endfunction endclass class err_test extends base_test; `uvm_component_utils(err_test) function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); my_driver::type_id::set_type_override(err_driver::get_type()); // before env is built super.build_phase(phase); endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The override target must extend the original type, or the factory reports an error. - Overrides must be installed before the `create()` they affect (parent before child in top-down build). - `create()` still calls `new()` internally; the factory just chooses *which* class's `new()`. ### Follow-ups - *Why is the constructor signature fixed?* The factory calls `new(name, parent)` for components and `new(name)` for objects; extra mandatory arguments break factory creation.

**Key idea:** No. UVM is a class library written *in* IEEE 1800 SystemVerilog (and standardized as IEEE 1800.2). It relies on SV classes, parameterized types, virtual interfaces, dynamic processes, mailboxes, and constrained randomization, so it only runs on a simulator that supports SystemVerilog. ```mermaid flowchart TB SIM["SystemVerilog simulator
VCS, Questa, Xcelium, Riviera"] --> SV["IEEE 1800 SystemVerilog
classes, interfaces, randomize, fork"] SV --> UVM["UVM library (uvm_pkg)
IEEE 1800.2"] UVM --> TB["your testbench
agents, sequences, tests"] ``` ### Explanation | UVM feature | SystemVerilog feature it uses | | --- | --- | | Components, objects, inheritance | classes, `virtual` methods | | Factory | parameterized classes, static members | | Sequences and constraints | `rand`, `constraint`, `randomize()` | | Phases, objections | `fork`/`join`, events, processes | | Pin access | virtual interfaces, clocking blocks | | TLM FIFOs | mailboxes | | `uvm_hdl_*` backdoor | DPI-C | ### Code ```systemverilog // Every UVM testbench starts by importing the SV package `include "uvm_macros.svh" import uvm_pkg::*; module tb_top; initial run_test(); // SV initial block starts UVM phasing endmodule ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - UVM methodology *ideas* (agents, scoreboards, constrained random) exist in other languages, e.g. cocotb/pyuvm in Python or UVM-SystemC, but those are separate implementations, not the SV UVM library. - Some simulators need a flag to compile the bundled UVM (e.g. `-ntb_opts uvm` or `-uvm`); the DPI part (`uvm_hdl_*`) needs the C library or `+define+UVM_NO_DPI`. ### Follow-ups - *Can you use UVM with a VHDL DUT?* Yes, through a mixed-language simulator; the testbench itself is still SystemVerilog.
chipverify-005:
**Key idea:** Registration is not mandatory, but it is what makes a class *creatable by the factory*. Once registered with `` `uvm_component_utils `` / `` `uvm_object_utils ``, the class can be built with `type_id::create()`, overridden by type or instance from a test, and created by name (`+UVM_TESTNAME`), which is how testbenches stay reusable.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test build_phase
  participant F as uvm_factory
  participant E as env build_phase
  T->>F: base_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type())
  E->>F: base_drv::type_id::create("drv", this)
  F-->>E: err_drv object (env code unchanged)
```

### Explanation
Registration gives you:
- `type_id` proxy (`uvm_component_registry`/`uvm_object_registry`) for `create()`.
- Type and instance overrides without editing the environment.
- Creation by string name: `run_test()` builds the test named by `+UVM_TESTNAME`.
- `get_type_name()`; with field macros also `print`, `copy`, `compare`, `pack`.

| Not registered | Registered |
| --- | --- |
| `new()` only | `create()` + overrides |
| `+UVM_TESTNAME=my_test` fails: "cannot create a component of type my_test" | test found by name |
| Swapping a driver means editing env code | one override line in the test |

### Code
```systemverilog
class base_drv extends uvm_driver #(bus_item);
  `uvm_component_utils(base_drv)            // registration
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
  endfunction
endclass

class err_drv extends base_drv;
  `uvm_component_utils(err_drv)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
  endfunction
  // inject errors in run_phase
endclass

class err_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(err_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
  endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    base_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type());
    super.build_phase(phase);
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Parameterized classes use `` `uvm_component_param_utils ``/`` `uvm_object_param_utils `` (no string-name lookup).
- Registering but then calling `new()` defeats overrides.

### Follow-ups
- *Cost of registration?* A static proxy object per class; negligible.
chipverify-006:
**Key idea:** An **active** agent builds a sequencer, driver, and monitor and drives the DUT interface. A **passive** agent builds only the monitor (and often coverage), so it observes the interface without driving it. The mode is the agent's `is_active` field (`UVM_ACTIVE`/`UVM_PASSIVE`), usually set through `uvm_config_db`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph ACT["active agent"]
    SQR["sequencer"] --> DRV["driver"]
    MON1["monitor"]
  end
  subgraph PAS["passive agent"]
    MON2["monitor"]
  end
  DRV -->|drives| IF1["interface A"]
  IF1 --> MON1
  IF2["interface B (driven by RTL)"] --> MON2
  MON1 -->|ap| SCB["scoreboard / coverage"]
  MON2 -->|ap| SCB
```

### Explanation
| | Active | Passive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Components | sequencer, driver, monitor | monitor only |
| Drives pins | yes | never |
| Typical use | block-level stimulus | internal bus at SoC level, output side of a DUT, reuse when another block drives the bus |

### Code
```systemverilog
class apb_agent extends uvm_agent;
  `uvm_component_utils(apb_agent)
  uvm_sequencer #(apb_item) sqr;
  apb_driver  drv;
  apb_monitor mon;
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
  endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    super.build_phase(phase);              // uvm_agent reads "is_active" from config_db
    mon = apb_monitor::type_id::create("mon", this);
    if (get_is_active() == UVM_ACTIVE) begin
      sqr = uvm_sequencer#(apb_item)::type_id::create("sqr", this);
      drv = apb_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);
    end
  endfunction
  function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    if (get_is_active() == UVM_ACTIVE)
      drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export);
  endfunction
endclass

// In the env/test, before the agent is built:
// uvm_config_db#(uvm_active_passive_enum)::set(this, "env.slave_agt", "is_active", UVM_PASSIVE);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Connecting `drv` in a passive agent dereferences null; guard `connect_phase`.
- Starting a sequence on a passive agent's sequencer fails because it does not exist.
- Default is `UVM_ACTIVE`; forgetting the config at SoC level gives two drivers fighting RTL.

### Follow-ups
- *Why keep a passive agent at all?* The same monitor, checks, and coverage are reused at system level with no stimulus code.
chipverify-008:
**Key idea:** Both macros register a class with the UVM factory; which one you use depends only on the base class. `` `uvm_component_utils `` is for classes derived from `uvm_component` (created with a name and a parent, part of the hierarchy). `` `uvm_object_utils `` is for classes derived from `uvm_object` (items, sequences, configs: created with a name only). Neither is "better"; using the wrong one does not compile correctly. ```mermaid flowchart TB O["uvm_object"] --> SI["uvm_sequence_item / uvm_sequence / config"] O --> CMP["uvm_component"] CMP --> DRV["driver, monitor, agent, env, test"] SI -.->|uvm_object_utils| R1["uvm_object_registry #(T)
create(name)"] DRV -.->|uvm_component_utils| R2["uvm_component_registry #(T)
create(name, parent)"] ``` ### Explanation What the macros give you (both): - A `type_id` typedef (the registry proxy) so `T::type_id::create()` works and overrides apply. - `get_type()`, `get_object_type()`, and `get_type_name()` (used in messages and by-name overrides). - Creation by string name (e.g. `+UVM_TESTNAME`). - The `_begin`/`_end` forms add field automation (`print`, `copy`, `compare`, `pack`, `record`). | Macro | Base class | Constructor | Variants | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `` `uvm_component_utils(T) `` | `uvm_component` | `new(string name, uvm_component parent)` | `_param_utils`, `_utils_begin/_end` | | `` `uvm_object_utils(T) `` | `uvm_object` | `new(string name = "T")` | `_param_utils`, `_utils_begin/_end` | ### Code ```systemverilog class my_item extends uvm_sequence_item; rand bit [7:0] data; `uvm_object_utils_begin(my_item) `uvm_field_int(data, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_object_utils_end function new(string name = "my_item"); // default name required for factory super.new(name); endfunction endclass class my_monitor extends uvm_monitor; `uvm_component_utils(my_monitor) function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction endclass class my_fifo #(int W = 8) extends uvm_component; `uvm_component_param_utils(my_fifo #(W)) // parameterized: no name lookup function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - An object without a default constructor argument (`new(string name)` with no default) cannot be created by the factory. - Field macros are convenient but slow; many teams hand-write `do_copy`/`do_compare`. ### Follow-ups - *Why do components need a parent?* The factory builds the hierarchy path from it, which instance overrides and config_db use.
chipverify-009:
**Key idea:** A sequence runs when something calls its `start(sequencer)` task (directly, via `` `uvm_do `` on a sub-sequence, or as a sequencer's `default_sequence`). `start()` binds the sequence to the sequencer, calls `pre_start`, `pre_body`, `body`, `post_body`, `post_start`, and returns when `body()` finishes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test run_phase
  participant S as my_seq
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  T->>S: seq.start(env.agt.sqr)
  S->>S: pre_start, pre_body
  S->>Q: start_item(req) (arbitration)
  S->>Q: finish_item(req)
  Q->>D: get_next_item
  D-->>Q: item_done
  Q-->>S: finish_item returns
  S->>S: post_body, post_start
  S-->>T: start() returns
```

### Code
```systemverilog
class my_seq extends uvm_sequence #(my_item);
  `uvm_object_utils(my_seq)
  function new(string name = "my_seq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    repeat (10) begin
      req = my_item::type_id::create("req");
      start_item(req);
      if (!req.randomize()) `uvm_fatal("RAND", "randomize failed")
      finish_item(req);
    end
  endtask
endclass

class my_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(my_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    my_seq seq = my_seq::type_id::create("seq");
    phase.raise_objection(this);
    seq.start(env.agt.sqr);       // 1) explicit start (recommended)
    phase.drop_objection(this);
  endtask
endclass

// 2) from a parent sequence:      `uvm_do(child_seq)   // create + start on m_sequencer
// 3) default sequence (no code in run_phase):
//    uvm_config_db#(uvm_object_wrapper)::set(this, "env.agt.sqr.main_phase",
//                                            "default_sequence", my_seq::get_type());
```

| Way | When |
| --- | --- |
| `seq.start(sqr, parent, priority, call_pre_post)` | most tests and virtual sequences |
| `` `uvm_do ``/`` `uvm_do_with `` inside a sequence | quick sub-sequences/items |
| `default_sequence` via config_db | phase-based starting without test code |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Nobody raised an objection: run_phase ends at time 0 and the sequence never runs.
- `start(null)` works only for virtual sequences that never call `start_item`.
- `start()` with default arguments calls the child's `pre_body`/`post_body`; `` `uvm_do `` starts sub-sequences with `call_pre_post = 0`, so those hooks are skipped.

### Follow-ups
- *What does start_item block on?* Sequencer arbitration grant (and `lock`/`grab` ownership).
